study_identification_part.si4_title: Normative modeling of brain morphometry in self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To quantify individual deviations from the normative range of brain morphometric variation in children with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) and to assess their associations with clinical manifestations and cognitive functions.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores; infra-normal defined as z < -1.96 (5th percentile); supra-normal defined as z > 1.96 (95th percentile); median range defined as -1.96 ≤ z ≤ 1.96; total number of regions with infra- or supra-normal deviations
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly defines the deviation metrics. Z-scores were calculated as (Y - Ŷ) / σ. Infra-normal and supra-normal deviations were defined using ±1.96 thresholds. The study also counted the number of regions with abnormal deviations for each participant.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: The normative deviation for each regional morphometric measure was defined as the z-scores: [formula] where Y represents the observed value and Ŷ represents the predicted value. A positive or negative z-score signifies that the predicted value of the corresponding morphometric measurement lies above or below the normative mean, respectively. In accordance with previous literature (ENIGMA Clinical High Risk for Psychosis Working Group et al. 2024), we defined regional non-normal z-scores as infra-normal when they fell below -1.96 or supra-normal when they exceeded 1.96, corresponding to the 5th percentile and 95th percentile, respectively. The median range (z-scores between -1.96 and 1.96) were classified as within the normal range.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group comparisons using 2-proportion z-tests for proportions of participants with deviations; two-sample t-tests for normative z-scores and observed measures; Spearman correlation for associations between number of regions with abnormal deviations and clinical manifestations; Pearson correlation for associations between averaged deviations and clinical manifestations; support vector classification (SVC) with linear kernel and 5-fold cross-validation to compare classification performance between z-scores and observed measures; FDR correction applied for multiple comparisons; significance threshold P < 0.05. Clinical variables examined: disease duration, seizure frequency, Raven's total score (cognitive function).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Children with SeLECTS exhibited a higher proportion of regions with infra-normal deviations in subcortical volume compared to controls, and the number of regions with normative deviations correlated with disease duration, seizure frequency, and cognitive performance (Raven's score).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found that children with SeLECTS exhibited a significantly higher proportion of regions with infra-normal deviations in subcortical volume compared to healthy controls (34.2% vs 18.5%, χ²=7.54, P=0.04 with FDR correction). No significant group differences were found in regional percentages of abnormal deviations for cortical thickness or surface area. Within the SeLECTS group, the number of regions with supra-normal deviations in subcortical volume was positively correlated with disease duration (R²=0.06, P=0.05) and seizure frequency (R²=0.11, P=0.01). The number of regions with infra-normal deviations in cortical thickness was positively correlated with Raven's total score (R²=0.07, P=0.05). The averaged regional z-scores of surface area were positively correlated with seizure frequency (R²=0.06, P=0.001). Classification models using either normative z-scores (AUC=0.56) or observed morphometric measures (AUC=0.48) failed to distinguish SeLECTS from controls effectively. Almost all participants had averaged normative deviations within the normal distribution, indicating that extreme deviations were present in only a minority of individuals. The authors concluded that regional morphometric variations in children with SeLECTS were nested within normal variation, highlighting individual-level heterogeneity.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Small sample size limiting generalizability of normative models; cross-sectional design not capturing longitudinal changes; models may underestimate age-related brain changes; only age and sex included as covariates, excluding demographic, developmental, and lifestyle factors
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, our study could benefit from the inclusion of a larger sample of children, which would result in more stable and generalizable normative models. Secondly, the morphometric measures were based on cross-sectional and did not capture longitudinal changes. Studies have shown that cross-sectional models and brain measures may underestimate the extent of age-related brain changes (Di Biase et al. 2023). Future normative model training and application should consider incorporating both longitudinal and cross-modal data. Thirdly, the model only considers sex and age, and demographic, developmental, and lifestyle factors were not included in the analysis.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study employed the CentileBrain framework specifically adapted for Chinese pediatric population (ages 3-18 years) rather than using the full lifespan model. Sex-specific models were developed separately for males and females. The study examined associations with functional gradient organization, hypothesizing that variation in neuroanatomical measures may be embedded within the brain's functional gradient architecture. Classification analysis compared performance between normative deviations and raw observed measures, finding both performed poorly, suggesting individual heterogeneity rather than consistent group-level differences. The study emphasized that extreme distributions were present in only a minority of individuals, highlighting the importance of individual-level analysis over group comparisons.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents an application of normative modeling to a relatively benign, self-limited pediatric epilepsy syndrome. The finding that group-level differences were minimal but individual heterogeneity was present aligns with the self-limited nature of the condition. The positive correlation between number of regions with infra-normal cortical thickness deviations and better cognitive performance (higher Raven's scores) is counter-intuitive and may warrant further investigation. The devCCNP dataset used for training is publicly accessible at https://ccnp.scidb.cn. The case-control data is available upon request. Cognitive assessments (Raven's and Integrated Visual and Auditory Continuous Performance Test) were administered to only 75 of the 187 SeLECTS participants. Clinical information (disease duration, medication duration/dose, seizure frequency) had missing data for some participants (indicated by footnote 'a' in Table 1). The study received approval from ethics committees at both Jinling Hospital (ID: 2018NZKY-020-02) and Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IDs: H15001, H15045, H22068).
